source_description: Arthur O. Lovejoy manuscript notebook; faint front-leaf title ‘Symbolism’ [?]

batch.method: Manual visual correction against rendered PDF pages, using PaddleOCR-VL only as a scaffold.
policy: Preserve Lovejoy's argumentative distinctions and readable terminology.
Do not infer manuscript pagination where a page label is not visibly secure.
Loose slips and back-matter memoranda are recorded as physically distinct note types.
Do not silently normalize difficult ethnographic names, multilingual titles, or compressed bibliographic references.
Where handwriting is too poor for diplomatic transcription, retain only source-supported argumentative structure and mark uncertainties.
batch.status: first pass complete; original-image second-pass corrections propagated for pp.117, 119 and 120; 2026-09-05 source/authorial-ceiling hygiene propagated for pp.106-119 without claiming new diplomatic completion

research_signals_from_batch: The pp.106–116 notes treat cannibalism, sacrifice, and initiation as problems of mechanism and classification, but many constituent categories are Marillier/Tylor/Frazer/Trumbull-field material; summary grammar is not authorial proof.

Ceremoniality, publicity, repetition, blood, pain, or an accompanying sacrifice do not by themselves establish one sacramental/sacrificial origin; exact Lovejoy-local application wording remains page-dependent where no W3 clause is registered.
Human sacrifice to water or hostile spirits is often classified as propitiatory and contrasted with communion feasts, but the component distinction is source-field material.

The general theory that animal sacrifice substitutes for an earlier human victim is questioned in the notes; exact wording and the relation to changing social/economic valuation remain incompletely diplomatic.

PDF p.112 preserves a strong case-level rejection/preference relation: circumcision is not accepted under a partial/substitute-human-sacrifice genealogy and is reallocated toward initiation, blood relation, fraternity and incorporation. The rival and preferred mechanism families are source-owned; exact rejection wording/source cue remains a diplomatic HOLD.

Whipping, scarification, seclusion, menstruation taboos, secret-society rites, and other initiation ordeals are compared through purification, fortification, social regulation, and group formation rather than automatically through sacrifice; most constituent mechanism categories are field-owned.

PDF p.117 is image-secure for a ranked synthesis: alimentary/anthropophagic cases are the greatest number; expiatory and quasi-judicial cases are the next most numerous; human sacrifice for union is altogether exceptional. Exact proposition authorship remains HOLD between a Lovejoy terminal synthesis and a lecture/source-derived conclusion.

Funerary companion-killing and burial of servants/retainers are treated as provision, communication, status-continuity, or propitiation for the dead, not necessarily mystical union; constituent mechanisms are source-field material.

PDF p.119 is W2–W3 for selected-body-part efficacy and a 'perh.' part-as-representative-of-whole explanation. Because the page is an undated late insert and both mechanisms are source-field available, the exact juxtaposition is an authorship-and-chronology HOLD, not a secure Lovejoy A2 fork.

PDF p.120 is a physically separate back-leaf memorandum. The top line reads ‘Recommence 5 Janvier’, followed by ‘Mardi à 11 h’; another line begins ‘special lecture Jan 9 ...’, and a final Marillier reference remains partly illegible.

pages.corrected_text:
The discussion turns explicitly to autophagy/anthropophagy as an interpretive problem. The notes pose whether eating human flesh is in itself a religious act. Repeated or customary cannibal practices can survive after their original motive has disappeared, so present ceremonial form is treated as poor evidence for original cause. Motives listed or compared include famine, revenge, hatred of enemies, affection for relatives, and acquisition of qualities attributed to the dead.

At the current evidence ceiling this is an editorial argument summary of a source-rich mechanism field, not a diplomatic Lovejoy-origin theory statement.

pages.corrected_text:
The notes distinguish collective/ritualized cannibalism from specifically religious or sacramental interpretations. Public feast, solemnity, repetition, or fixed ceremonial rule is treated as insufficient by itself to prove an original religious/sacramental motive; later ritual sanction may regulate an older practice.

The general anti-form principle is field-mediated. Any Lovejoy-local application depends on the exact manuscript wording, which remains incompletely diplomatic on this page.

Sacred animals and head/soul or body-part relations also enter the comparison.

The left page continues source criticism of cannibal evidence. A new heading on the right concerns human sacrifice used to propitiate the spirit of the victim in order to avert injury to the sacrificer. An African example treats a murdered or sacrificed person's spirit as potentially dangerous, with later offerings directed toward appeasing that victim-spirit rather than necessarily a pre-existing god.

The mechanism family is source-field material; exact authorial allocation on the page remains to be completed diplomatically.

pages.corrected_text:
Water-spirits and animal forms are compared with sacrifice to natural powers. Men thrown or cast into water may represent propitiation of a dangerous spirit rather than meal/communion sacrifice. The page also questions the general theory that animal sacrifice is simply a humane substitute for earlier human sacrifice; the current summary records few secure demonstrations and mentions changing social conditions or valuation of human life as another possible factor in decline.

Human→animal substitution itself is field-known. The exact evidential critique and social-valuation wording remain incompletely diplomatic.

pages.corrected_text:
Sacrifice to water deities or hostile spirits is compared with sacramental communion. A victim cast into the sea during violent danger is treated as propitiation; a contrasting communion/union model concerns a deity conceived as friend/protector. Similar outward forms can therefore be allocated to different mechanisms.

The propitiation-versus-communion distinction is already present in the contemporary sacrifice field; this page's exact local connective remains only partly diplomatic.
uncertain_readings: exact Lovejoy-authored contrast wording not fully recovered

pages.corrected_text:
Persons surviving attacks by tigers or other dangerous animals may be treated as ritually altered, impure, sacred, or specially related to a deity; this status need not imply sacrifice. The main topic then becomes circumcision. At the current high-confidence argument level, the page rejects a genealogy in which circumcision is interpreted as a partial/substitute human sacrifice and reallocates the rite toward initiation, fraternity/blood relation, incorporation, and admission to a social or religious group.

The rejected sacrifice genealogy and the blood-covenant/incorporation alternative both existed before Lovejoy; the local significance is the case-specific rejection/preference relation. Exact rejection wording, immediate source cue, and transition syntax remain diplomatic HOLDs.

pages.corrected_text:
Puberty rites are described in detail. At a girl's first menstruation a bullock may be sacrificed and a ritual dance performed, while the girl is secluded and temporarily removed from ordinary work and conversation. The notes place these restrictions alongside menstrual blood, danger, impurity, initiation, and changed social status rather than allowing the accompanying animal sacrifice alone to determine the mechanism.

The constituent initiation mechanisms are field-owned; exact local allocation wording remains partly crossed out/uncertain.

pages.corrected_text:
Beating, whipping, cutting, scarification, and other painful acts at initiation are compared. Explanations in which pain merely makes admonitions memorable are treated as insufficient; the packet also considers but does not accept as a general default an interpretation of whipping/bloodletting as partial sacrifice of the novice to a god. Comparative alternatives include ordeal, purification, bodily marking, group discipline, and production of a new social status.

The alternatives are source-field categories; exact page-level negative judgment wording remains incompletely diplomatic.
uncertain_readings: exact wording and scope of the anti-partial-sacrifice judgment incomplete

pages.corrected_text:
Initiation is further analyzed through purification and fortification. Flagellation and lustration can purge impurity or strengthen a novice at a dangerous transition. Comparative notes describe girls beaten with rods or thorn-wood until blood is drawn, menstruation restrictions, and secret-society initiation. Separation from ordinary life, bodily trial, secrecy, and readmission under changed status are compared against a presumed offering-to-deity explanation.

The current text remains a high-confidence mechanism summary rather than a full diplomatic transcription of every line.

pages.corrected_text:
The notes gather food, bodily-contact, sex, and menstruation taboos. Men and women may be prohibited from eating together, contact with menstruating women avoided, and young people segregated during maturation. The packet compares separation, protection, purity, social regulation, and possible group/blood-fraternity relations rather than automatically treating these taboos as sacrificial. A hypothesis about girls' initiation and durable relations among cohorts/complementary groups remains partly illegible.

Exact authorial phrasing of the group-bond hypothesis is not yet diplomatically secure.

[continuation:] Times it is even adults married men who are beaten. At all events, we have no reason for connecting [the] observance with human sacrifice. The idea in gt. number of cases is alimentary, i.e. a case of anthropophagy. In [the] next most numerous cases, it is expiatory & quasi-judicial. A human sacrifice for union is altogether exceptional, while the [illegible/abbrev.] sac. of union is more frequent than alimentary [illegible]. Of course we shall have presently to consider a number of actual examples; but they are none the less relatively rare.

Companion-killing, burial of servants, and sending wives or dependants with the dead are compared with alimentary, sacramental, utilitarian, status-preserving, expiatory, provision, and communication explanations. Slaves or retainers sent into graves or killed before burial can function in a continued-service/status-continuity model analogous to sending messages or useful goods to the dead.

These constituent funerary mechanisms are source-field material; exact local reclassification wording remains incomplete.
